newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines aims to cut armed forces.
newsitem.headline: Philippines aims to cut armed forces.

text.p: The Philippines hopes to reduce its military personnel by up to 21,500 men to 86,000 in 10 years as it acquires more arms, President Fidel Ramos said on Saturday.

"Changes in the major services should strive for an Armed Forces of the Philippines that is lean, compact and responsive," Ramos said in a speech on the 61st anniversary of the Armed Forces of the Philippines.
Ramos said the programme aimed to trim the country's armed forces by up to 20 percent and maintain a minimum defence capability for credible deterrence.

Of the 107,500 men comprising the Philippine armed forces, some 70,000 are in the Army, 22,100 in the Navy and 15,360 in the Air Force. They are supported by a 30,000-strong civilian militia called Citizen Armed Forces Geographical Units (Cafgu), latest data from the Department of Defence showed.

"Our soldiers...deserve the best equipment that the republic can afford," Ramos said. Besides an arms build-up, the programme includes the improvement of communication facilities of the military and the professionalisation of its ranks.

On Thursday, Congress signed a resolution appropriating an initial 50 billion pesos ($1.9 billion) to finance the first five years of the armed forces' proposed $12.75 billion modernisation programme for 15 years.

The programme, partly dictated by concerns about possible conflicts over the Spratly islands in the South China Sea, calls for the purchases of frigates, jet fighters, armoured vehicles and other weaponry.

The Spratlys are a cluster of isles, reefs and shoals believed to be sitting atop rich veins of gas and oil and are claimed wholly or in part by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
Ramos said said the modernisation of the country's armed forces was necessary to "respond credibly to any emergency or fortuitous eventuality, even one not necessarily military".

"Beyond the perennial challenge of ensuring national security, we have come to look to the armed forces of the Philippines as a force for building political stability, economic development and social progress," Ramos said.
Ramos recently forged a peace agreement with the mainstream Moro National Liberation Front ending a 24-year war for self rule in the south that killed 125,000 people.

The government is also holding talks with the Communist-led National Democratic Front on how to end the 27-year communist insurgency in the country. The insurgency has declined sharply with less than 5,000 fighters left from a peak of 26,000 in 1987.
